summary: Defines the clearance sponsor attribute, which records the entity that sponsored, or granted, a clearance. It is meant for certificates that also carry the clearance attribute. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If a badge lets you into a secret room, this adds a note saying who vouched for you to get that badge.

questions: who sponsored a clearance in a certificate
how to use clearance sponsor in authorization
subtitle: Recording who granted a security clearance in a digital certificate

tldr.problem: Digital certificates can include security clearance information, but they lack a way to record which organization or agency granted that clearance.
tldr.mechanism: The clearance sponsor attribute adds a text field (up to 64 characters) to certificates to name the entity that issued the clearance.
tldr.outcome: Systems can now verify who sponsored a clearance and use that information in automated authorization decisions, checking the sponsor against an approved list.

today: RFC 5917 is an Informational specification published in June 2010 and has not been obsoleted. It remains the definition of the clearance sponsor attribute for use in public key certificates and attribute certificates.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content:
RFC 5917 defines the clearance sponsor attribute, a new field for digital certificates. This attribute records the organization or agency that granted a security clearance to the person named in the certificate.

The clearance sponsor attribute works together with the clearance attribute, another certificate field that states what kinds of classified information a person is allowed to access. While the clearance attribute says what access is permitted, the sponsor attribute says which organization made that decision.
sections.eli5: A clearance attribute says you can read secret documents. The sponsor attribute says which government agency decided you could.

sections.title: The Sponsor Field
sections.content:
The clearance sponsor is stored as a text string using the UTF-8 character encoding. It can be anywhere from 1 to 64 characters long, and there is exactly one sponsor per certificate. If an employee gets clearances from different organizations, each clearance goes in a separate certificate with its own sponsor value.

The identifier for this attribute in the certificate is a unique number: 2.16.840.1.101.2.1.5.68. Systems compare sponsor values using case-insensitive matching, so 'Engineering' and 'engineering' are considered the same.
sections.eli5: The sponsor name is a short label (up to 64 characters) that says who vouched for the clearance. A certificate has just one sponsor.

sections.title: Using It for Authorization
sections.content:
When a web server or other system receives a user's certificate, it can check the clearance sponsor to decide whether to grant access. For example, the server might maintain a list of approved sponsors (such as 'Defense Intelligence Agency' and 'National Security Agency') and only allow users whose sponsor appears on that list.

This check happens alongside the normal validation of the certificate's digital signature and chain of trust. The mechanism for managing the approved sponsor list is not specified in this RFC; each organization decides how to maintain it.
sections.eli5: A server can look at who sponsored the clearance and check whether that organization is on the trusted list before letting the user in.

sections.title: Security Concerns
sections.content:
If the sponsor value is used in authorization decisions, the organization assigning the value must do so correctly. Because the sponsor field is stored in the certificate itself, including it there protects the value from being modified later: the certificate's digital signature confirms that the stated sponsor value was authorized.

However, the certificate issuer and the clearance sponsor may be different entities. If they are, there must be a secure way for the sponsor to tell the issuer that the clearance was granted. If the same sponsor name (such as 'MoD' for Ministry of Defence) is used by multiple countries' PKI systems, relying parties must distinguish them somehow, such as by also checking the issuer's identity.
sections.eli5: The sponsor name in the certificate is sealed by a digital signature, so nobody can change it after issue. But different countries might use the same sponsor name, so you need to know who issued the certificate too.

sections.title: Technical Requirements
sections.content:
The clearance sponsor attribute is defined using ASN.1, a formal notation for describing data structures. When implemented, it must follow these rules: only one clearance sponsor value per certificate, text must be encoded as UTF-8, and case-insensitive matching must be used when comparing sponsor values.

The RFC notes that DirectoryString values can technically include the NUL character (U+0000), but clearance sponsor values should not. Implementations that perform case-insensitive matching must check the entire string to prevent truncation attacks where an attacker cuts off part of a name.
sections.eli5: The sponsor field follows strict technical rules: one name per certificate, UTF-8 text only, and comparisons ignore uppercase/lowercase differences.
